issues.legal_issue: A qualifying tank fishery, including a right to fish in it, is retained by an intermediary rather than vesting in the State under the statutory vesting scheme.
material_facts: The lessors’ predecessor had obtained a permanent lease of the fishery right in a tank, without the subsoil, and the lessors later leased that right to the lessee.
The fishery was a reservoir or place for storing water used for fishing and satisfied the statutory explanation of a tank fishery.
The lessee argued that the fishery right was an encumbrance that ended when the intermediaries’ interests vested in the State.
issues.conclusion: The fishery qualified as a tank fishery, and even assuming the lessors were intermediaries, their interest in it did not vest in the State and was retained.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 4 and 6(1)(e) of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, section 6 permits an intermediary to retain a tank fishery despite the general vesting of intermediary interests under section 4. The explanation to section 6(1)(e) includes the right of fishing in a qualifying reservoir or place. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.statutory_vesting_dispute: The case concerns whether an interest held through an intermediary passes to the State under a statutory vesting scheme.
predicates.water_reservoir_used_for_fishing: The property is a reservoir or place for storing water that is used for fishing.

issues.definition: When a statutory vesting dispute concerns a water reservoir used for fishing, the rule treats the qualifying tank fishery as retained by the intermediary.

issues.legal_issue: Khas possession is not required for an intermediary to retain a tank fishery.
material_facts: The lessors had leased the fishery right to the lessee, so they were not themselves in actual possession of the fishery.
The statutory clause concerning tank fisheries did not specify khas possession, although another clause expressly required it for agricultural land.
Documents and government records described the lessors as tenants, and the government had accepted rent from them.
issues.conclusion: An intermediary need not have khas possession to retain a tank fishery; the lessors’ interest did not vest in the State on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6(1) of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, expressly requires khas possession for the property specified in clause (d), but clause (e) for tank fisheries contains no such requirement. The court also relied on records and the government’s acceptance of rent as recognition of the lessors’ tenancy status. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.statutory_vesting_dispute: The case concerns whether an interest held through an intermediary passes to the State under a statutory vesting scheme.
predicates.intermediary_claims_retention_of_tank_fi: An intermediary claims to retain an interest in a tank fishery.
predicates.property_not_in_khas_possession: The intermediary does not have actual possession of the property in question.

issues.definition: If an intermediary claims to retain a tank fishery in a statutory vesting dispute, the absence of the intermediary’s actual possession does not prevent retention.

issues.legal_issue: A lessee remains liable to pay rent to the lessors when the lessors’ interest has not been shown to end, notwithstanding the statutory vesting scheme.
material_facts: The lessee took the fishery under a lease granted by the lessors and claimed that the statutory vesting scheme had ended their interest and frustrated the lease.
The rent claim concerned years before the provisions of Chapter VI were given effect to.
The lessors’ interest in the tank fishery had not vested in the State, and the lessee did not show that the lessors’ title had subsequently ended.
issues.conclusion: The lessors retained their rights in the tank fishery and were entitled to recover the claimed rent; the appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5(1)(c) of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, provided that qualifying non-agricultural tenants, and until Chapter VI took effect qualifying raiyats, held their land directly under the State on the same terms and conditions as before vesting. The court held that this did not prevent recovery of the rent in dispute. It also applied the principle that a tenant who took a lease cannot deny the lessor’s title at the commencement of the tenancy unless the lessor’s title is shown subsequently to have ended. No earlier cases were relied on.

rule.if: appeal_from_rent_recovery_suit and lessee_took_property_under_lessors_lease and lessor_interest_not_shown_to_end and rent_period_precedes_later_tenancy_chapter

predicates.appeal_from_rent_recovery_suit: The proceeding is an appeal arising from a suit to recover rent.
predicates.lessee_took_property_under_lessors_lease: The person resisting rent took the property under a lease granted by the persons seeking rent.
predicates.lessor_interest_not_shown_to_end: No evidence shows that the lessors’ interest or title subsequently ended.
predicates.rent_period_precedes_later_tenancy_chapt: The rent claim concerns a period before later tenancy provisions were given effect.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a rent-recovery suit, a lessee who took the property under the lessors’ lease remains liable to them where their interest is not shown to have ended and the rent period precedes the later tenancy provisions.
